title: The 50 Percent Problem
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Benjamin Riley uses a large longitudinal study of roughly 27,000 Chinese secondary students to argue that unsupervised generative-AI use is quietly hollowing out learning even as it appears to help. Within five months of adoption, half of AI-using students had moved to what the researchers call full homework outsourcing, cutting their time on task by roughly a quarter while their homework scores rose. Riley's central move is to show that this apparent success was an illusion measured on the wrong instrument: the same students' performance on closed-book exams fell by about 20 percent, and their scores on high-stakes entrance exams dropped by 18 to 24 percent depending on the exam. He frames this as the clearest real-world evidence yet that AI-assisted homework can decouple the visible marker of achievement (a completed, well-scored assignment) from the underlying capability it is supposed to signal. The piece is pitched as a caution to AI optimists, including Riley himself, that positive homework data can actively conceal a decline in what students actually know and can do unaided.
points: Riley's key statistic — a 20 percent decline in closed-book exam performance despite higher homework scores — demonstrates that homework completion rates and grades are not reliable proxies for learning once AI is available to do the underlying cognitive work.

The finding that AI-using students spent noticeably less time on homework (about 45 minutes versus 60+ minutes) while scoring higher on it reframes 'AI efficiency' as a warning sign rather than a benefit when the task is meant to build durable knowledge.

The steep 18–24% drop in scores on China's high-stakes entrance exams for long-term AI users gives the 'homework outsourcing' problem real stakes: it is not just a classroom-management issue but one that can measurably affect a student's long-run academic trajectory.
quotes: Approximately 80% of students adopted generative AI, with half engaging in full homework outsourcing within five months.
Students using AI spent significantly less time on homework (around 45 minutes vs. 60+ minutes for non-users).
While AI-using students initially received higher homework scores, they performed substantially worse on closed-book exams — experiencing a 20% average performance decline.
High-stakes college entrance exam scores dropped 18% for long-term AI users; high school entrance exams declined 24%.
The study found no evidence of any corresponding learning benefit arising from students using AI.
